chunks: Brushless vs brushed advantages. The question: What are some advantages of brushless vs brushed motors?
A brushed motor switches its coil current with a sliding contact (brushes). A brushless motor does the same job with electronic switches.
Nearly every advantage of brushless comes from removing that sliding contact: longer life, better efficiency, less noise, and higher speed and power.
The price is a more complex controller.
Think of two doors. One has a rubbing seal that scrapes the floor each time it swings, so it wears out, squeaks and wastes effort. The other opens with no contact at all.
The brushed motor is the scraping door, and the brushless motor is the contactless one.
The analogy has one gap: the contactless door needs a smart control system, just as a brushless motor needs a controller.
Every brushed-motor limitation traces back to one of two root causes: the sliding contact (the four-way branch on the left) and having the hot winding on the rotor (the pair of boxes on the right).
Commutation: switching the coil current as the rotor (the spinning part) turns. Mechanical in a brushed motor, electronic in a brushless one.
Brush wear: the slow loss of brush material by rubbing and sparking. EMI: unwanted electrical noise that disturbs nearby circuits.
Contact voltage drop: the voltage lost where the brushes touch the commutator, typically about 1–2 volts for the pair.
Power density: how much power you get for the motor's size and weight.
Suppose the two brushes together drop about 1 volts, the low end of the usual range. On a 12 volts motor, 1 / 12 is roughly 8% of the input power lost at the brushes.
On a 3 volts motor, the same 1 volts is 1 / 3, about 33% . A brushless motor has no brush drop, so it wastes none of it. It also needs no brush replacement.
The cost is a controller: a set of electronic switches, a way to sense the rotor's position, and software to run them.
That is the whole idea: removing the sliding contact fixes wear, loss and noise.
"Brushed motors commutate mechanically; brushless motors commutate electronically, and nearly every advantage follows from that.
No brushes means no wear, so longer life, no arcing, so less EMI and no sparks, and no brush friction or voltage drop, so higher efficiency.
The winding sits on the stator against the housing, so it cools better and handles more continuous power, and top speed isn't limited by the commutator.
The cost is the controller: a three-phase bridge, sensing and firmware, so brushed is still the cheap, simple choice for low-duty or low-cost applications."
